persona.bio: Tara, 25, social media manager at a regional chain of bakeries. She runs Instagram, Facebook and TikTok, plans posts in a shared Google Sheet, answers comments and DMs every morning, writes captions for every new product, pulls numbers for a monthly report and coordinates photo shoots with the store managers by email in Gmail. She has never used AI; her manager is not sure what the company allows.

path.role: You’re the social media manager for a chain of bakeries, handling captions, comments, scheduling, messages, emails and the monthly report.

steps.firstStep: I’m a social media manager for a bakery chain. I write Instagram and Facebook captions every day. Write one caption for this post, in a warm, cheerful voice, under 40 words, with one emoji at most and two relevant hashtags. Here is what the post is about: [paste the photo details and the key facts here].

steps.note: I am the social media manager for a chain of bakeries. I write captions, reply to comments and messages, and send emails to customers and to my team. My readers are neighbors and regulars who love fresh bread and pastry, so I keep things warm, short and friendly, with a light touch of charm. Captions stay to a few lines. Replies are one or two sentences. Never add details I did not give you, like prices, hours, flavors or promotions. If something is missing, put it in square brackets and ask me. Do not use hype words. Give me one draft, and I will read and change it before anything goes out.

steps.title: Your post captions, with a saved assistant
steps.read: Your captions now come from a Claude project that already knows your bakeries, your voice and your habits. You tell it what is in the photo and when to come in, and it drafts the caption for you to read. That is better in your job because every post sounds like you without starting from a blank page each day.

material.label: Instructions for your assistant
items: I am the social media manager for a chain of bakeries. You write post captions for our Instagram and Facebook in my voice. Our voice is warm, short and a little playful, like a friendly baker talking to a neighbor. Captions run two to four short lines. I will usually give you a photo description, what the item is and when people should come in. Start with the item or the moment, not with a greeting. Use sensory words like flaky, warm or buttery only when they fit what I told you. Never invent prices, flavors, hours, locations, deals or ingredients I did not give you. If something is missing, put it in square brackets and tell me what you need. Do not use hype words. Avoid long hashtag lists. At most add two or three simple hashtags if I ask. Give me three caption options each time, and say which one is the shortest. I will read and change everything before it is posted.

material.label: Examples to start with
items: Flaky layers, butter rich, and a little bake sitting by the window. Come in before 10 and grab one warm.
Fresh [item] just came out of the oven. They are best in the first hour, so come say hi before [time].
[Item] is back this week. Soft inside, golden outside, and ready when you are at [location].

steps.title: Your comment replies, saved once on your phone
steps.read: Your common comment replies now live on your phone’s keyboard. You type a few letters and the whole reply appears, ready for you to adjust. That is better in your job because comments come in all day, and your answers stay warm and consistent without typing each one again.

material.label: Your replies
items: Thank you so much! We are so glad you enjoyed it. Hope to see you again soon!
Great question! You can find the details at [location or link]. Let us know if you need anything else.
We love hearing that. I will pass your kind words on to the bakers!
Thanks for letting us know. I am sorry about that. Could you send us a message with the details so we can look into it?
Yes, we do have it! Availability can change, so please check with [location] before you come.
Thank you for tagging us! We love seeing it.
Come see us at [location]. We would love to have you!

safeUse: Never type customer names, phone numbers, emails or home addresses into Claude. Use square brackets instead.
Never paste private messages or complaints that include a customer’s personal details.
Keep your company’s sales numbers, internal plans and staff schedules out of the chat unless your manager says it is fine.
Check every price, hour, flavor and ingredient against your own approved sources, especially anything about allergens.
Read every caption and reply before it goes out, and change anything that does not sound like you.
steps.askMessage: Hi [manager or IT contact], I would like to know which AI tools the company has approved and what I may use them for. I am thinking of using one to draft post captions and to write replies to comments, and later to plan weekly content, answer messages and write emails. I would also like to know whether I may link my work email to an AI tool, and if not, which of these tasks should wait for your OK. I will read everything before it goes out and keep customer details out of it. Could you let me know what is allowed?

design.today: You write these about once a day, each one from scratch. You start from the bakers' photos and last week's posts.
design.newWay: You keep a saved assistant that already knows your bakery voice and how your best captions sound. For each new post you give it a few words about the bake and the photo, and it drafts a caption in your style. You read it, change anything that is off, and post it yourself. Your voice stays the same from day to day and you stop starting from a blank page.

steps.goal: Check with your company whether you may use AI for your work, and do not paste anything from work until you have an answer.
Get ChatGPT ready on your phone and computer so you can use it where you work.
Pick five or six of your best past captions, including the croissant one, to show the assistant your voice.
Build a saved assistant for captions that holds your voice notes and example captions.
Try it on the next real post and adjust the instructions until the caption sounds like you.

material.label: Caption assistant instructions
material.what: Tells the assistant that it writes short, warm Instagram and Facebook captions for a chain of bakeries, and how to use the details you give it.

material.label: Tone notes
material.what: Describes your voice, such as the cozy, playful feel of your croissant caption, plus words and habits you like or avoid.

material.label: Example captions
material.what: Holds your best past captions so the assistant can copy your style.

material.label: Post details prompt
material.what: A short fill-in form for the bake, the photo, the time of day and any offer, like coming in before 10 for a warm one.

design.checkPoint: You read each caption and check every name, time and offer before you post it yourself.

design.today: You reply to comments one by one as they come in.
design.newWay: You save your most common replies, such as thanks, opening hours and where to find a bake, so a reply is a few letters away on your phone. For comments that need more thought, you ask your assistant for a draft in your voice. You read each reply and send it yourself. Replies sound friendly and consistent, and you spend your attention on the comments that matter.

steps.goal: Check with your company whether you may use AI for your work, and keep customer names and private details out of any tool until you know.
List your ten most common comment replies, such as thanks, opening hours, allergy questions and sold out answers.
Save those replies so each one is a few letters away when you answer comments on your phone.
Build a saved assistant for trickier comments that drafts a reply in your voice from the comment text.

material.label: Tone notes

design.checkPoint: You read every reply before you send it, and nothing is posted by itself.

You pick one and fix it, so the voice stays the same and the blank page goes away.

design2.newWay: You save answers to the questions you get most, like hours, orders and allergens, as shortcuts on your phone. When a message comes in you insert the right answer and change what needs changing. Repeat questions go quickly and you keep your time for unusual ones.

steps.goal: Ask your company whether you may use AI tools for work before using AI to word your saved answers.
Save your most common message answers as text shortcuts on your phone keyboard.
